TranscriptSegments.Content: What stood out to you from the week?
I took the Thursday break.
I almost did not.
I had the calendar reminder and I remember staring at it like it was asking me to do something irresponsible.
What helped you go anyway?
I thought about the example from last week.
My supervisor had not punished me for giving a realistic timeline.
I told myself 10 minutes outside was not going to destroy the day.
And what happened?
Nothing dramatic.
I walked around the block, came back and finished the email I had been avoiding.
I was less frantic.
I keep waiting for these things to feel profound, but mostly they feel ordinary.
Ordinary can be valuable.
You are learning that a pause does not have to be earned by reaching a breaking point.
I did it again on Friday.
That one was harder because I had a client situation that was upsetting.
I wanted to stay at my desk until I solved everything.
What did you notice before you made that choice?
I was holding my breath again.
I had that thought that if I stopped paying attention, something bad would happen.
But I knew I was not actually doing useful work.
I was just rereading my notes.
Were you able to check the evidence for that thought?
A little.
The client had been connected with the right person.
I had done what I could do that day.
I still felt worried, but I could see that worrying was not the same as being needed at that exact second.
That is a meaningful distinction.
It also made me think about my dad.
When he got sick, it felt like there was always one more call to make.
If I stopped paying attention, I was afraid I would miss something important.
It makes sense that stepping away can carry more meaning than simply taking a break from work.
I had not connected those things before.
With my dad being organized felt like love.
If I forgot something, I felt like I had failed him.
And now when you are responsible for people at work, the same rule may be showing up.
Staying vigilant is how you prove you care.
Yes, except I cannot keep doing it all the time.
I am tired of making every task feel moral.
That is a powerful way to put it.
Caring about your work does not require treating every unanswered message as a test of your character.
I want to believe that.
I am not sure I know what caring looks like without overextending myself.
We can learn it gradually.
What happened with Nora this week?
We cooked dinner together on Wednesday.
I did not open my laptop afterward.
I told her I was trying to keep the evening separate from work, and she said she had noticed I seemed more present.
How did it feel to hear that?
Nice.
And then sad.
I did not realize how absent I had been.
Part of me wanted to apologize for every time I was in the room, but not really there.
You can acknowledge the impact without turning the whole history into evidence against yourself.
That is hard for me.
My first instinct is always to make a list of everything I did wrong.
What might it be like to make room for both truths?
You have been strained and less available at times, and you are taking steps to reconnect now.
Less punishing, more honest, maybe.
How have the darker thoughts been since we last spoke?
They have not come up this week.
I have had moments of feeling overwhelmed.
But I did not feel like disappearing from everything.
Do you have any plan or intention to harm yourself today?
No, I do not.
Thank you We will continue to check in directly.
What would you like to practice between now and next week?
I want to keep the Thursday break, but I also want to try leaving work on time one night.
Even saying that makes me nervous.
What is the smallest version of that experiment?
Tuesday.
I can leave by 6, even if my list is not finished.
I can write down the first thing I will do the next morning, so I am not carrying it all evening.
That sounds specific.
What might you say to yourself when the guilt arrives?
Maybe leaving work does not mean I stopped caring.
It feels corny, but it is probably true.
It does not have to sound perfect to be useful.
We can review what you notice.
OK, I think I am starting to see the pattern before it takes over.
Not every time, but sometimes.
Sometimes is a real beginning.
You mentioned in your note that leaving work on time was harder than taking a short break.
What happened Tuesday?
I packed my bag by 6.
Then an email came in from a client who was upset about a hearing date.
I told myself I would only respond for 5 minutes.
An hour later, I was still there.
What made it difficult to leave after you had already prepared to go?
The client sounded scared.
I know the date was not something I could change that night, but I felt like leaving would mean I did not care.
What did caring require in that moment?
I could have sent a short response saying I received the message and would call the next morning.
That would have been enough Instead, I researched everything again because I wanted to make the fear go away for both of us.
And could you make the fear go away?
No, I was just more tired.
I sent a longer email, and then I worried I had said the wrong thing.
It sounds like urgency pulled you away from the boundary you had planned.
I keep seeing that I confuse being available with being helpful.
What is the difference for you?
Being available means I respond immediately and make the person feel I am there.
Being helpful means I do the next appropriate thing, even if it is not everything they want in that second.
That is a thoughtful distinction.
Could you practice a version of that response in advance?
Maybe.
I received your message.
I know this is stressful.
I will review the details and call you tomorrow.
It sounds almost too simple.
Simple can be clear and containing.
It also tells the client what to expect without promising work you cannot complete well at the end of the day.
I worry they will think I do not care.
What evidence do you have that a measured response means you do not care?
None, really.
I think I am imagining how I would feel if I were scared.
But I would probably rather get a clear answer tomorrow than a rushed answer tonight.
That is useful empathy, not a reason to abandon your limits.
Nora said something similar.
She told me, I speak about my clients as if I am the only thing between them and disaster.
I was defensive at first.
What did you hear in what she said?
That I take my job seriously in a way that can make me feel alone.
I do not want to be told to care less.
But maybe I need to remember there are systems and colleagues and other resources too.
You can care deeply without becoming the whole system.
I want to write that down.
Please do.
How was it to notice the grief moments we discussed?
I had one on Thursday.
I was organizing a file and remembered how my dad used to keep every receipt in a labeled envelope.
I got unexpectedly emotional.
I went to the bathroom and cried for a few minutes.
What happened after you let yourself feel it?
I felt embarrassed, but also calmer.
I did not need to work faster afterward.
I came back and did one task at a time.
That is important information.
Letting the feeling exist did not make you incapable of continuing.
No, it actually made the day feel less sharp.
Would you like to keep making room for that when it comes naturally?
Yes, not on a schedule, just without treating it like a problem to solve.
That sounds wise.
